The Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Common Sense Group, Dr Olumide Emmanuel, has faulted state governors over Nigeria’s persistent electricity crisis, saying they have no justification for failing to improve power supply despite increased revenues and the authority to generate electricity. Emmanuel, speaking during an interview with select journalists in Lagos, said state governments should be held accountable for the continued darkness across the country, arguing that the financial resources available to them and recent electricity sector reforms should have translated into improved power supply for residents. The entrepreneur assessed the economic reforms of the President Bola Tinubu administration, particularly the removal of petrol subsidy and the floating of the naira. According to him, the governors have received increased allocations following the removal of the subsidy but have failed to translate the additional revenue into tangible improvements in the lives of Nigerians. He said, “For the state, for instance, every state has now been given power to produce its own electricity. Why are we still having power problems? What are the governors doing with the money? “If we are not going to hold these governors accountable, we will continue in this situation. “Because, like I have said over and over again, I don’t believe that any political party is the solution to our issue in Nigeria. So, I believe in being factual and realistic about it. Why do governors have that kind of money and they cannot have electricity? People should no longer be in darkness right now,” he stated Emmanuel argued that the benefits of the Federal Government’s economic reforms had largely remained at the macroeconomic level, with many Nigerians yet to experience meaningful improvements in their daily lives. The Common Sense Group chief executive said state and local governments should take greater responsibility for delivering essential services, including electricity, education, healthcare and transportation. He maintained that the responsibility for translating increased government revenue into improved living conditions rested largely with state and local governments rather than the Federal Government alone. On the broader energy sector reforms, Emmanuel questioned the failure to revive Nigeria’s government-owned refineries almost four years after the removal of the petrol subsidy. The subsidy has been removed. Is there any refinery, apart from the Dangote Refinery, that is working? “So what is now happening? If there was no Dangote, what would they have been doing? They have removed subsidy for four years, and up to now, Port Harcourt refinery is not working, Warri is not working, Kaduna is not working. And then we have not been able to build any new one,” he stated. He contrasted the government’s inability to restore the state-owned refineries with the progress made by the private sector, citing the Dangote Petroleum Refinery as an example of what could be achieved with investment in domestic refining. Emmanuel said the refinery had strengthened Nigeria’s position amid global energy supply challenges, noting that the country could have faced a more difficult situation without the facility. He attributed part of the refinery’s development to the government’s decision to remove the petrol subsidy and efforts to support local refining. He, however, insisted that the Federal Government must address the shortcomings in the implementation of its reforms, particularly the failure to restore the country’s public refineries and ensure that the benefits of subsidy removal reach ordinary Nigerians. Emmanuel also called for greater accountability in public spending, arguing that unnecessary government expenditure on official vehicles, foreign trips and renovations could be redirected towards critical infrastructure. He said the country should reconsider its growing borrowing appetite, particularly when government spending could be better prioritised. On electricity, he maintained that the states had a responsibility to deploy their increased revenues towards improving power infrastructure and ensuring residents had access to reliable electricity. He added that Nigerians should shift their attention from the Federal Government to state governors and local government chairmen, whom he described as critical to delivering the benefits of economic reforms at the grassroots.
